newsitem.title: GERMANY: Iran in the dock in German murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Iran in the dock in German murder trial.

text.p: A Berlin judge rules on Thursday whether one Iranian and four Lebanese were responsible for the gangland-style killing of a group of Kurdish Iranian dissidents by two masked men with machineguns in 1992.

But the real drama will focus on whether judge Frithjof Kubsch names the men whom the prosecution says ordered and approved the shootings -- Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.

At stake are relations between Iran and Germany, its biggest trading partner and most important friend in the West. Bonn has doggedly insisted on maintaining amicable relations with Tehran while its major allies accuse the Iranians of state terrorism.

German prosecutors put out an arrest warrant more than a year ago for Iran's Intelligence Minister Ali Fallahiyan whom they accuse of masterminding the attack in Berlin's Mykonos restaurant on September 17, 1992.

Iran denies any part in the killings and blames internecine feuding for the deaths of Sadegh Sharafkandi, exiled leader of the Iranian Democratic Party of Kurdistan (DPK-I), two fellow officials and their translator.
But the prosecutors allege Fallahiyan hired an Iranian grocer living in Berlin, Kazem Darabi, to organise the attack.

They are asking for life sentences for murder for Darabi and Abbas Rhayel, a Lebanese accused of being one of the gunmen. Three other Lebanese face possible jail sentences of between five and 11 years for complicity.
Iran has made clear that it objects to such attacks on its reputation and said on Wednesday proceedings would begin soon against 24 German firms reported to have helped Iraq to make chemical weapons.
Bonn is bracing for repercussions. Depending on the trial's outcome, a wholesale review of bilateral ties may be necessary, the Foreign Ministry says.

Ministry spokesman Martin Erdmann said ambassadors from the European Union's 15 states met an Iranian Foreign Ministry official to seek assurances the security of Germans and other Europeans in Iran would be guaranteed.

He said the official had repeated assurances given by Foreign Ministry Ali Akbar Velayati, saying that Iran would continue to meet its international commitments and ensure the security of Germans living in Iran.
Velayati was quoted earlier by that Iranian daily Kayhan as saying "a negative verdict by the Mykonos trial will have a negative impact on political and economic ties between Tehran and Bonn."

But he denied that pro-Iranian groups might attack German interests or German nationals in Iran. "These are nothing but baseless allegations...We support human values and German nationals will have full security," he said.

Media reports say a government working group expects Iran's reaction to the judgment to be limited if Tehran is mentioned only in general terms but much more severe if Rafsanjani or Khamenei is named.
The Bonn government repeated its call to Germans not to go to Iran unless absolutely necessary, and then to stay in constant touch with the embassy.
When prosecutor Bruno Jost last November accused Khamenei of ordering the killings, a mob marched on Germany's embassy in Tehran, hurling eggs and stones and calling for Jost's death.

Iran is particularly incensed that the prosecution bases much of its case on the testimony of former president Abolhassan Banisadr and Abolhassem Mesbahi, until recently an international trouble-shooter for Tehran and now, like Banisadr, a fugitive from its wrath.
Mesbahi said written orders for killings such as those in Berlin were issued by a secret Council for Special Operations, chaired by Khamenei, and would be approved by Rafsanjani.
